analysis.one_liner: Opens protected federal ocean waters to oil and gas drilling and stops future marine national monuments.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal law so that most areas of the outer Continental Shelf — the federal waters off the U.S. coast — could not be set aside from oil and gas drilling except by an Act of Congress. It would have wiped out existing presidential withdrawals of those waters from leasing (keeping only sanctuaries and already-declared monuments), barred presidents from creating new marine national monuments, and limited emergency suspensions of drilling operations to 90-day stretches. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never moved again [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to large swaths of federal offshore waters for exploration and drilling. Gulf Coast energy industry jobs and revenue could grow. The bill's sponsor is from Louisiana, a drilling-heavy state.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so that no unleased shelf land may be withdrawn from oil and gas disposition except by an Act of Congress, with presidential withdrawal power limited to national marine sanctuaries [S3].
It rescinds existing withdrawals from leasing except for areas in national marine sanctuaries or national monuments [S2][S3].
It bars the President from declaring any ocean waters or seabed as a new national monument, while leaving already-declared monuments untouched [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, coastal communities and fishing and tourism industries would have faced expanded drilling off their coasts, and future permanent marine protections would have required an Act of Congress rather than presidential action. Taxpayers would also bear the environmental and cleanup risks that come with expanded offshore production.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have ended permanent presidential protection of federal ocean waters, meaning any future withdrawal for conservation or national-security reasons would need a full Act of Congress [S3].
It would have prevented presidents from establishing new marine national monuments, foreclosing a tool used in past decades to set aside sensitive ocean areas [S2][S3].

Any suspension of drilling operations under a war or national emergency would be capped at 90-day renewable periods rather than an indefinite suspension, a change that would limit flexibility in an actual crisis [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a single industry — offshore drillers — while the costs are broad and hard to reverse: expanded drilling risk to coasts, fisheries, and tourism, and a permanent narrowing of federal power to protect ocean areas. Even a supporter of drilling would have to concede the monument prohibition and the rescinding of existing withdrawals are significant and long-lasting changes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in April 2017, and the committee never held a vote on it; the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 27, 2017, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1][S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any hearing in the committee, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill had only its sponsor and one other cosponsor, both Republicans from Louisiana [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism industries, and conservation interests are better off because the bill never moved; the existing withdrawals of federal waters from drilling would have been rescinded under this bill. No oil and gas company gained access to new federal waters as a result.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to open federal offshore waters to drilling and bar new marine national monuments

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore energy
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred on April 27, 2017

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were attached to the bill, both Republicans from Louisiana, and no votes ever occurred, so no party-line pattern can be measured [S1][S4].

industries.note: The bill would have rescinded existing withdrawals from federal waters and made future withdrawals require an Act of Congress, opening large new areas to drilling. It never became law, so drillers gained nothing and the status quo held [S2][S3].
These industries benefit from existing protections keeping drilling out of broad areas of federal ocean waters. The bill's failure left those protections intact [S3].
